enrichment.short_title: DPP case stated remission refused in racially aggravated POA appeal
key_facts: A 16-year-old was acquitted by Mid Kent Youth Court of racially aggravated threatening behaviour; co-defendants pleaded guilty.
The DPP appealed by case stated, arguing the justices were wrong on the facts found, particularly that the respondent was unaware of co-defendants' racial hostility.
Late applications sought remission to delete paragraph 6(v) of the case as unsupported by evidence; skeleton argument and CCTV were lodged very late.
The DPP conceded that on the case as stated the appeal would fail because guilt could not be established even on joint enterprise.
Events dated from March 2002 and significant delay had occurred without fault of the respondent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from the Youth Court to the High Court (Administrative Court).
enrichment.outcome: Application to remit the case stated to the justices refused; appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Although the High Court has jurisdiction under section 28(A)(2) of the Supreme Court Act 1981 to remit a case stated for amendment, it will refuse remission where the appeal raises no question of general principle, the appellant did not take the evidential point in the appellant's notice, delay is substantial and not the respondent's fault, and justice does not require reopening fact-finding many months after the trial.
legal_issues: Whether the case stated should be remitted to amend a finding that the respondent was unaware of racial hostility expressed by co-defendants
Whether there was no evidence for the finding in paragraph 6(v) or no reasonable bench could have made it
Whether CCTV evidence could be admitted on a case stated hearing
Whether delay and lack of public importance justified refusing remission

notes: Leading intervention/HRA proportionality analysis; Peter Smith J reasoning overturned.

enrichment.short_title: Law Society intervention justified despite HRA Article 1 challenge
key_facts: Mr Holder, a sole practitioner, was intervened in by the Law Society in June 2001 after an OSS inspection revealed missing client account records, a £200,950 client account shortfall, substantial moneylender debts, and letters potentially misleading the Compensation Fund.
He applied under Schedule 1 paragraph 6(4) to set aside the intervention; Master Price dismissed the claim and Peter Smith J allowed appeal on Human Rights Act grounds.
Peter Smith J held intervention could infringe peaceful enjoyment of possessions and suggested court-appointed receivers as a fairer alternative.
The Law Society appealed; intervention in about 100 practices per year was said to be at stake.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against an order allowing the solicitor's challenge to a Law Society intervention notice.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Master's order dismissing the claim restored.
enrichment.ratio: Law Society intervention under the Solicitors Act 1974, though draconian, falls within the legislature's margin of appreciation under Article 1 of the First Protocol; the court must assess an individual intervention by the statutory procedure laid down by Parliament, not by comparing it to a hypothetical receiver remedy devised by the court, and where intervention is entirely justified on the facts the balance of public interest and the solicitor's interests is properly struck.
legal_issues: Whether Law Society intervention infringes Article 1 Protocol 1 peaceful enjoyment of possessions
Whether the court may substitute a receiver appointment for statutory intervention
Application of margin of appreciation to professional regulation
Whether Article 6 required legal aid where accounts were frozen
Whether lack of immediate urgency undermined the intervention

notes: Long commercial judgment on marine reinsurance disclosure; market practice central.

enrichment.short_title: Marine quota-share retrocession and no-loss warranty fax
key_facts: Groupama sought payment under a marine personal accident quota-share retrocession treaty from Overseas Partners Re (OP), with AON as brokers.
OP increased participation from 50% to 75% subject to a warranty that there were no losses incurred on the programme to date.
AON faxed on 29 June 1998 confirming no losses advised that would affect declarations; words 'to LDG' were deleted before sending.
Four losses had been reported to Lloyd's by that date; a $28,000 net Cobb loss had eroded a deductible but had not been passed down the chain.
OP argued AON should have inquired up the chain; Groupama argued market practice limited disclosure to losses advised to the reinsured.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Commercial Court on liability for unpaid reinsurance claims and avoidance for misrepresentation or non-disclosure.
enrichment.outcome: Claim allowed against OP; claim against AON dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Read together, OP's June fax requesting warranties as to losses incurred on the programme and AON's response that no losses had been advised affecting the declarations meant losses reported to the reinsured (Ray Smart), not all losses known anywhere in the placement chain; market practice did not require brokers to inquire of Lloyd's placing brokers unless losses had been advised downstream, and the undeclared Cobb loss was immaterial to a prudent underwriter in the context of the programme.
legal_issues: Construction of the 18 and 29 June 1998 faxes on losses incurred versus losses advised
Whether a warranty request extended the duty to inquire up the reinsurance chain
Whether four Lloyd's-reported losses made AON's statement untrue
Materiality and inducement under section 18(2) of the Marine Insurance Act 1906
Whether avoidance for a variation avoids the whole contract or only the variation

enrichment.short_title: ASBO prostitution appeal adjourned for respondent representation
key_facts: The Chief Constable of Lancashire appealed by case stated against refusal to grant an ASBO against Lisa Potter, alleged to be a prostitute operating in a Preston residential area.
Other respondents' cases were severed and held in abeyance pending this appeal.
The respondent did not attend before the district judge; solicitors Inghams had acted but faxed on 21 January 2003 that they had no recent instructions and would not appear.
The court was concerned the respondent might not know of the hearing and that important issues of construction and burden of proof under section 1 would be decided without adversarial argument.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from the magistrates' court; hearing adjourned on the court's own initiative.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal adjourned; directions for service on respondent and possible Attorney General advocate to the court if she did not instruct solicitors within seven days.
enrichment.ratio: Where a case stated raises issues of general importance on the construction of ASBO legislation and turns significantly on hearsay evidence, and the respondent may be unaware of the hearing despite solicitors having previously acted, the High Court may adjourn rather than hear a one-sided appeal, with directions for personal service and, if necessary, appointment of an advocate to the court under the Attorney General's scheme.

Appropriate burden of proof under section 1(1)(a)
Admissibility and weight of hearsay evidence before the district judge
Fair hearing where respondent's solicitors withdraw shortly before the appeal

enrichment.short_title: First section 115 clearly unfounded asylum certification cases

statutes_considered.title: Convention relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: ZL and VL, Czech Roma family members, claimed asylum on arrival on 8 November 2002 and were processed at Oakington under the new section 115 regime.
Claims were rejected and certified as clearly unfounded on 14 November 2002, before the 2002 Act was promulgated on 28 November.
Section 115(6) requires certification for listed accession states unless the Secretary of State is satisfied the claim is not clearly unfounded, blocking in-country appeal.
Expert evidence on Czech Roma conditions and prior IAT decisions in Puzova were before the court.
VL returned voluntarily to the Czech Republic after the hearing; ZL disclosed a rape allegation after the initial decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed applications for permission to seek judicial review of asylum refusal and section 115(6) certification, following refusal by Goldring J.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; permission to seek judicial review refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 115 certification of clearly unfounded asylum claims from listed states is an objective test applied by considering the claim against known country background; the Oakington fast-track procedure affords a fair opportunity to show an arguable case; use of section 115 before promulgation of the Act was unfair in principle but cured here by full review on the merits; for Czech Roma the general sufficiency of state protection means most claims will be clearly unfounded though individual cogent persecution evidence may still succeed.
legal_issues: Fairness of certifying claims under unpromulgated legislation
Procedural safeguards for section 115 asylum processing at Oakington
Construction of 'clearly unfounded' and section 115(6) mandatory certification
Whether Czech Roma asylum claims could be clearly unfounded given country evidence
Article 8 family life where husband retained in-country appeal rights

notes: Youth court identification appeal; Forbes pure recognition exception applied.

enrichment.short_title: PACE Code D pure recognition and Turnbull identification
key_facts: H, aged 16, was convicted in the Youth Court of assault occasioning actual bodily harm on AS, aged 15, at St Leonards-on-Sea railway station.
AS had known H for about 18 months; H denied involvement and disputed identification.
No identification parade was held; PC Berry considered it futile because the girls knew each other.
The magistrates admitted the identification evidence and found AS credible and H evasive.
The case was stated on Code D compliance and sufficiency of recognition evidence alone.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from East Sussex Youth Court to the High Court.
enrichment.outcome: Questions answered in favour of the magistrates; conviction upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where a witness purports to recognise a defendant well known to her over 18 months and neither defendant nor her solicitor requests a parade or puts recognition in issue at interview, an officer may justifiably treat the case as pure recognition under R v Forbes and need not hold a Code D parade; if the code was complied with, section 78 exclusion is not required unless Turnbull directions show the evidence unsafe, and a magistrates' court may convict on recognition evidence alone if sure the identification is accurate.
legal_issues: Whether failure to hold an identification parade breached Code D paragraph 2.3
Whether the Forbes pure recognition exception applied
Whether identification evidence should have been excluded under section 78 PACE
Whether guilt may rest on the victim's recognition evidence alone

notes: CCRC referral; supergrass corroboration distinguishes safe conviction.

enrichment.short_title: Supergrass conviction safe despite Serious Crime Squad taint
key_facts: Anne Marie Murray was convicted in April 1989 of attempted robbery of Patricia McGowan, relying principally on supergrass Paul Jarvis.
Jarvis was handled by West Midlands Serious Crime Squad officers later discredited; the judge warned the jury that Jarvis was an accomplice witness requiring corroboration.
Murray was acquitted on related handling and burglary counts where corroboration was lacking but convicted on count 15 where Mrs McGowan's evidence supported Jarvis's account of inside information.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred the case because the prosecution rested almost entirely on Jarvis.
Jarvis implicated Murray in November 1987 before police knew of any link between Murray and McGowan.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction following reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission.
enrichment.ratio: Alleged police misconduct and unreliability of a supergrass in other cases does not automatically taint every conviction in which he testified; where the jury convicted only where independent evidence corroborated Jarvis, and the independent evidence on the attempted robbery (McGowan's banking routine and car details known to Murray) was not fed to Jarvis by compromised officers and remains unimpugned, the conviction remains safe under Pendleton.
legal_issues: Whether Paul Jarvis's discredited status and linked officer misconduct rendered Murray's conviction unsafe
Whether independent corroboration from Mrs McGowan insulated the conviction
Whether the jury's acquittals on other counts showed proper caution
Application of tainted evidence principles from Edwards, Gall, Lynch, Dunne and Treadaway

notes: Interlocutory libel applications; trial listed; justification amendment allowed.

enrichment.short_title: Slander qualified privilege and late Lucas-Box justification
key_facts: Birchwood Homes and directors Steen and Minerva sued councillor Robertson for slander at a meeting with resident Moira Gill on 8 March 2002.
Robertson called Birchwood a fraudulent business from second-hand car dealing; the conversation was secretly video-recorded by private detective Anthony Rich.
Robertson pleaded qualified privilege; claimants sought Part 24 summary judgment on privilege and opposed Robertson's late application to add justification.
Proposed Lucas-Box meanings were that Steen conducted affairs dishonestly and aggressively and Birchwood was not to be trusted.
Particulars relied on 1990 Cycletec and Magna Marketing schemes and recent Heald proceedings involving alleged forgery.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications before trial: Part 24 summary judgment on qualified privilege and permission to amend defence to plead justification.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to amend to add justification granted; Part 24 application on qualified privilege refused.
enrichment.ratio: A councillor advising a constituent about a proposed local development may have qualified privilege even if he says he speaks as a friend rather than as councillor, and an ex tempore remark does not automatically defeat privilege under Horrocks v Lowe; defamatory allegations in the words complained of are not automatically justifiable under US Tobacco and Cruise unless severable and distinct from the pleaded meanings, but here fraud and aggression were linked in context and justification may be pleaded; Burstein does not require striking out mitigation background on a set-up allegation at this stage.
legal_issues: Whether Robertson's 'speaking as a friend' remark destroyed qualified privilege
Whether privilege required the defamatory words to be in response to an enquiry
Whether aggression in the words complained of was severable for Lucas-Box justification
Whether late justification particulars were adequate under McPhilemy
Whether Part 24 summary judgment on privilege was bound to succeed

notes: Split on Hay grading issue in judgments but appeal dismissed on all points.

enrichment.short_title: Race discrimination in auditor appointment and Hay grading
key_facts: Temibola Afolabi, a black African auditor, was interviewed for Auditor Grade SO2 in 1990 but appointed at Grade 6 while a less experienced white candidate with CIPFA Part I was also appointed at Grade 6.
He brought a second complaint in July 1999 after discovering Mr Dusu's interview notes on his personnel file.
He also complained that in 1999 Hay grading treated him less favourably than white departmental auditors Jordan and Draper.
Hay evaluated Afolabi and the comparators' jobs at grade 9; Southwark did not inform or implement his regrading for months while comparators were later regraded higher.
The employment tribunal extended time by nine years and found direct racial discrimination on both complaints; the EAT dismissed Southwark's appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission against Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissal of employer's appeal from an employment tribunal race discrimination decision.
enrichment.ratio: An employment tribunal may justly extend time under section 68(6) where the applicant only discovered an arguable case on inspecting his personnel file within three months of issuing proceedings, even after nine years' delay, if prejudice is balanced; failure to answer a section 65 questionnaire may support an inference of discrimination; on Hay grading, events after April 1999 including failure to implement grade 9 and more favourable treatment of white comparators could support an inference of continuing less favourable treatment on racial grounds within the pleaded issue of failure to regrade.
legal_issues: Whether it was just and equitable to extend time for a 1990 non-appointment claim
Whether Southwark directly discriminated in failing to appoint Afolabi to Grade SO2
Effect of failure to respond to a race relations questionnaire
Whether Hay grading discrimination was pleaded or went beyond the defined issue
Comparator analysis and inference drawing under King v Great Britain-China Centre

notes: Urgent possession stay application; fraud challenge must be fresh action.

enrichment.short_title: Mortgage consent order fraud challenge misconceived in CA
key_facts: Victor Francis Harper obtained a £150,000 mortgage in 1989; possession was ordered in April 1996 after arrears accumulated.

The Court of Appeal granted permission to appeal in June 1998 on disputed fines and interest charges; the appeal was compromised by consent on 12 May 1999 capitalising debt at £182,000 and staying enforcement for Harper's lifetime.
Harper died in March 2001; executor Corbett Harper sought to set aside the consent order alleging false accounting and perjured evidence.
County court applications to set aside the Court of Appeal order were dismissed for lack of jurisdiction; a Grepe v Loam order was made.
Bradford & Bingley held a warrant for possession of Woodfield House, Birmingham.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent without-notice application to the Court of Appeal to set aside a 1999 consent order and stay a warrant for possession.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused as misconceived; short stay until Tuesday 28 January 2003 for vacating only.
enrichment.ratio: An allegation that a Court of Appeal consent order was obtained by fraud cannot be raised by application in the possession proceedings or directly to the Court of Appeal without a separate action to establish the fraud; Wood v Gahlings requires such matters to be investigated at first instance, and James v Williams confirms fraud must have materially contributed to the impugned order—here the executor must explain the reduction from earlier debt figures to the £182,000 compromise and quantify any cross-claims before a stay could be justified.
legal_issues: Whether the Court of Appeal has jurisdiction to set aside its own consent order for fraud on without-notice application
Whether liberty to apply in the consent order permitted setting it aside
Whether alleged false accounting vitiated the 1999 compromise
Whether misselling or unquantified cross-claims justified staying possession
Effect of death on the lifetime stay under the consent schedule
